title: Centripetal Acceleration and Centripetal Force
notes:
## 1. Topic Introduction — The Force That Bends Motion

Uniform circular motion needs an acceleration even though the speed never changes — because the *direction* of velocity changes every instant. That inward acceleration, and the force behind it, governs every turning car, whirling stone and orbiting satellite.

## 2. Fundamental Concepts (NEB 2023, 2024)

### 2.1 Definition

**Centripetal acceleration** is the acceleration of a body in uniform circular motion, directed along the radius **towards the centre**, of magnitude $a_c = \dfrac{v^2}{r} = \omega^2 r$. **Centripetal force** is the net force producing it: $F_c = \dfrac{mv^2}{r} = m\omega^2 r$.

### 2.2 Derivation of $a_c = v^2/r$ (the 5m NEB derivation)

Consider a particle moving with constant speed $v$ in a circle of radius $r$. In a short time $\Delta t$ it moves from A to B, sweeping angle $\Delta\theta$; the velocity vector rotates from $\vec v_A$ to $\vec v_B$ by the same angle $\Delta\theta$.

1. $|\vec v_A| = |\vec v_B| = v$; the chord AB has length $AB = v\Delta t$ (arc ≈ chord for small $\Delta\theta$).
2. The arc subtended: $AB = r\Delta\theta$ (small-angle), so $v\Delta t = r\Delta\theta$.
3. The change in velocity $\Delta\vec v = \vec v_B - \vec v_A$ forms a triangle similar to the (isosceles) triangles in the geometry: the velocity triangle with sides $v, v, \Delta v$ is similar to the position triangle with sides $r, r, AB$.
4. Hence $\dfrac{\Delta v}{v} = \dfrac{AB}{r} = \dfrac{v\Delta t}{r}$, giving $\dfrac{\Delta v}{\Delta t} = \dfrac{v^2}{r}$.
5. In the limit $\Delta t \to 0$: $a_c = \dfrac{v^2}{r}$, directed along the radius towards the centre (since $\Delta\vec v$ points inward as $\Delta\theta \to 0$).

With $v = r\omega$: $a_c = \omega^2 r$. Force: $F_c = ma_c = \dfrac{mv^2}{r} = m\omega^2 r$.

**Key properties:** $F_c$ is *not a new kind of force* — it is the name for whatever real force plays this role (tension, gravity, friction, normal force).

### 2.3 Worked numericals

**Q (3m, 2022 & 2024):** Car, r = 50 m, v = 10 m/s: $a_c = v^2/r = 2$ m/s²; $F_c = m \times 2$ per unit mass; $\omega = 0.2$ rad/s.

**Q (NEB-style):** A 0.5 kg stone is whirled on a 1 m string at 4 m/s. Find the tension.
$T = mv^2/r = 0.5 \times 16/1 = 8$ N.

## 3. Conceptual Relationships

- **To Topic 23:** $a_c = v^2/r = \omega^2 r$ — the two forms.
- **To Topic 26/27:** at the top of a vertical circle and on banked roads, gravity/friction/normal supply $F_c$.
- **To Newton's second law:** $F_c = ma_c$ is just $F = ma$ applied along the radius.
- **"Centrifugal force"** is a rotating-frame artifact, not a real force — in an inertial frame only the inward force exists.

### 4.2 Model answer skeleton for the 5m derivation

Definition (1m) → diagram with A, B, $\vec v_A$, $\vec v_B$, $\Delta\theta$ (1m) → similarity of triangles / chord relation (1m–2m) → $\Delta v/\Delta t = v^2/r$ (1m) → direction towards centre + $F_c = mv^2/r$ (1m).

### 4.3 Common examination mistakes

1. Calling centripetal force a separate force acting outward/inward in addition to tension or gravity.
2. Deriving with the full arc length instead of the small-angle approximation.
3. Omitting the direction (towards the centre) — the definition is incomplete without it.
4. Using $v = \omega r$ with inconsistent units.

summary: In uniform circular motion the speed is constant but the velocity vector rotates, so an acceleration must act: **centripetal acceleration** $a_c = v^2/r = \omega^2 r$, always directed to the centre. The derivation (NEB 2023, 2024, 5m) uses the similarity between the velocity triangle and the position triangle: $\Delta v/v = v\Delta t/r$, hence $a_c = v^2/r$. The net inward force $F_c = mv^2/r$ is not a new force — tension, gravity, friction or the normal force plays the role. A car on a 50 m turn at 10 m/s needs $a_c = 2$ m/s² supplied by road friction (NEB 2022, 2024); a stone on a 1 m string at 4 m/s needs 8 N of tension. "Centrifugal force" is only a rotating-frame bookkeeping device.
specialNotes: Always identify which real force provides the centripetal force — never add 'centripetal force' as a separate force in the FBD.
Centrifugal force is a pseudo-force — it appears only in rotating reference frames, not in inertial frames.
If the centripetal force is removed, the body moves tangent to the circle (Newton's first law).
Maximum-speed problems: set F_c = mv²/r equal to the maximum available force (tension, friction) and solve for v.
NEB frequently asks: 'Find the maximum speed' — use v_max = √(μ_s rg) for curves, v_max = √(T_max r/m) for strings.

simulation.title: Centripetal Force Visualizer
simulation.description: Animate a particle moving in a circle. Visualize velocity (tangential), centripetal acceleration (inward), and the net centripetal force. Vary radius, speed, and mass to see how F_c = mv²/r changes. Toggle between string, gravity, and friction scenarios to see how different real forces provide the centripetal force.
outputs: T (tension) or f (friction) or F_g (gravity) — identifying the real force
Period T = 2πr/v — time for one revolution
visualElements: Particle orbiting in circle with velocity arrow (tangential, blue)
Force arrow pointing to center (green), labeled with source (Tension/Gravity/Friction)
Real-time graph: F_c vs v, F_c vs r, F_c vs m
Scenario selector: string, planet orbit, car on flat curve, banked curve

details: Changes direction of v, not magnitude
NOT a new force — it is a ROLE
Provided by: tension, gravity, friction, normal
Car on road: friction provides F_c
Banked road: normal force component provides F_c
Set F_c equal to maximum available force
Centripetal force is not added to FBD
If F_c removed → body moves tangent

specificConditions: **Inertial/Non-Inertial Distinction:** Centripetal force is a real resultant force in an inertial frame; it is not a 'fictitious' force. Fictitious centrifugal force only appears in the rotating reference frame to maintain Newton's laws.

**Directional Constraint:** Centripetal force must act strictly perpendicular to the instantaneous velocity for the speed to remain constant. If the net force has a tangential component, the speed changes (non-uniform circular motion).
**Radius Variation:** If the path radius $r$ changes during the motion, the centripetal force requirement $F_c = mv^2/r$ must adjust instantaneously based on the new radius and speed at that instant.
